frame: PER-ANCHOR — read each record's own `frame` field, which is either "mean" (precession only) or "true" (nutation included). The two anchors here deliberately differ, because their sources do. See frame_note; this is the single most dangerous field in the file.
description: The Lahiri (Chitrapaksha) ayanamsa: the angle subtracted from a tropical longitude to obtain a sidereal one. Every body in a sidereal chart moves by exactly this amount, so an error here is a rigid rotation of the whole chart — it changes signs and houses wholesale while leaving every INTER-body relationship (aspects, patterns, dignities by mutual angle) untouched. That is the precise shape of fault the golden vectors cannot see, because both engines rotate together and keep agreeing. A1's generative harness has already found one real bug in this frame (sidereal whole-sign cusps, session 25b), which is why ACQUISITION.md §4 prioritises this anchor.
frame_note: MEAN vs TRUE is not a detail; it is a ~14-17 arcsecond systematic, larger than every other tolerance in this directory combined. The MEAN ayanamsa counts precession alone. The TRUE ayanamsa adds nutation in longitude, which oscillates within roughly ±17.2 arcsec on an 18.6-year period. The value recorded here is MEAN. Swiss Ephemeris must therefore be asked for its mean ayanamsa (nutation suppressed) when it is compared against this file — comparing a true ayanamsa to this anchor produces a confident, plausible-looking failure of up to 17 arcsec that has nothing to do with the engine being wrong. This repository has already been bitten once by the same distinction in a different place: the backend's fixed-star frame offset is computed as a tropical-minus-sidereal Sun difference precisely BECAUSE get_ayanamsa_ut disagreed with the chart longitudes by the nutation term.

anchors.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 arcsec. NOT the source's printed precision, which is 5 decimal places of an arcsecond and would imply a nonsensical ±0.000005 arcsec. The honest uncertainty here is dominated by single-secondary-source risk: the constant appears in one peer-reviewed paper which attributes it to the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris rather than reproducing an IAE page directly, and which is demonstrably careless elsewhere (see retrieval_note). It is trusted to ~0.5 arcsec because it independently reproduces a value it was not fitted to — the 1956 Calendar Reform Committee definition — to within 0.56 arcsec. It is not trusted to its printed digits.
anchors.engine_allowance_note: 1 arcsec. Swiss Ephemeris and the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris are documented to adopt slightly different base values for the same nominally-Lahiri ayanamsa, so two correct implementations of 'Lahiri' legitimately differ at about this level. 1 arcsec is 1/60 of the 1 arcmin at which a longitude error becomes capable of flipping a sign or house assignment, so this allowance cannot mask a chart-visible error. If the engine misses by MORE than uncertainty + allowance, that is a finding to investigate, never a number to widen — see README.md.
anchors.source: Bishnupriya Pani, Deepak K Pattanaik, Nachieketa K Sharma, 'A Comparative Analysis of Different Types of Ayanāṃśa in Ancient Indian Astronomical Computations', Orissa Journal of Physics (Orissa Physical Society), ISSN 0974-8202, Vol. 31, No. 2, August 2024, pp. 133-143, at p. 136
anchors.citation: It is reliably learnt that Indian Astronomical Ephemeris (IAE) have adopted the above formula from year 1985 onwards (omitting the third component i.e.: 0.000113×T^3, the value being insignificant) for calculating mean Ayanāṃśa, for use in their Ephemeris, taking C value as 85885.53192 seconds. [4,5]
anchors.retrieval_note: Retrieved as PDF and read directly, not via a search-engine extract. Two cautions are recorded deliberately rather than smoothed over. (1) The paper is a SECONDARY source: it attributes the constant to the IAE (refs [4,5]) and hedges with 'it is reliably learnt', rather than reproducing an IAE page. The IAE itself is a print publication of the Positional Astronomy Centre, Kolkata (India Meteorological Department) and puts no values online — its official page confirms the publication and that its ephemerides are argued in terrestrial time, but prints no constants. (2) The SAME paper is unreliable in its worked examples: at pp. 138-139 it computes 'Lahiri' by a linear 50.29 arcsec/year from a 285 AD zero-point, obtaining 24.3068° for 2025 — identical to its Raman figure, and irreconcilable with the official Chitrapaksha definition. Those derived example values are explicitly NOT used here. Only the quoted IAE constant is taken, and only because it survives the independent check below.
anchors.validation: Accepted on the ordering ACQUISITION.md §Verification requires: validated BEFORE this repository's engines were consulted, and against a value it was not fitted to. Propagating this constant back to the Indian Calendar Reform Committee's definitional epoch with the IAE's own stated formula (P = C + 5029.0966T + 1.11161T² − 0.000113T³, T in Julian centuries from J2000) gives a MEAN ayanamsa of 23° 14' 43.889" at 1956-03-21 00:00. The CRC fixed the ayanamsa at 23° 15' 00" at that epoch — a gap of +16.11 arcsec. Nutation in longitude at that same instant, by Meeus' low-accuracy series (Astronomical Algorithms ch. 22, ~0.5 arcsec accurate), is +16.67 arcsec. Residual: −0.56 arcsec, inside that series' own accuracy. The gap is therefore the mean/true distinction and not an error in the constant. The same relation holds at the other end: this mean value minus the −14.03 arcsec nutation at J2000 gives a TRUE ayanamsa of 23° 51' 11.5", matching the 23° 51' 11" widely published for Lahiri at J2000. One constant predicting two independently published values it was not derived from is what earns it a place here; a transcription slip would not do that.

anchors.epoch: 1956 vernal equinox — the Calendar Reform Committee's defining instant
anchors.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 arcsec, for secondary-source risk rather than printed precision — the figure is quoted to a milliarcsecond but reaches this file through a secondary account of the decree rather than through the Report of the Calendar Reform Committee itself. The 1955 decree and its 1985 revision differ by 0.658 arcsec, so anyone citing 'the' official value can legitimately mean either; 0.5 arcsec keeps that ambiguity from being papered over while staying far below the point where it could hide a chart-visible error.
anchors.engine_allowance_note: 1 arcsec, same basis as lahiri-mean-j2000: two faithful implementations of the same official Lahiri definition legitimately differ at about this level.
anchors.source: Indian Calendar Reform Committee decree (Government of India, 1955), as reported in R. Scott, 'The "Lahiri ayanamsha" and the Sidereal Zodiac'
anchors.citation: the ayanamsha was decreed to be 23°15'00" on March 21, 1956, 0:00 ET but was later revised in 1985 to be 23°15'00.658", a true value which includes nutation and is relative to the true equinox of-date.
anchors.retrieval_note: SECONDARY source, retrieved and read directly (not a search-engine extract). The primary Report of the Calendar Reform Committee was not obtained — it is a 1955 Government of India / CSIR print publication. This record is kept anyway, at a tolerance that respects its provenance, because its INDEPENDENCE is worth more here than its precision: see independence_note. The quoted sentence is also the source of this anchor's `frame`, which it states outright rather than leaving to be inferred — 'a true value which includes nutation'. That matches, and was predicted by, the nutation analysis recorded under lahiri-mean-j2000.
anchors.independence_note: This is the anchor with teeth, and the reason it exists. lahiri-mean-j2000 agrees with Swiss Ephemeris to under a MILLIarcsecond — 0.000 arcsec of margin used out of 1.5. Exact agreement that total is not the reassurance it looks like: it is equally consistent with the two being faithful implementations of one specification, and with the published constant having been sourced, somewhere up its citation chain, from Swiss Ephemeris itself — which is precisely the circularity ACQUISITION.md §4 warns against, restored by the back door. That question could not be settled by inspection: the vendored Swiss build is compiled WASM, and the published Swiss documentation does not print its Lahiri base constant. THIS anchor settles it instead, by construction. A 1955 governmental decree cannot have been derived from Swiss Ephemeris, so the engine reproducing it is evidence that could not have come from circularity. It does reproduce it: 23° 15' 00.796" against the decree's revised 23° 15' 00.658", a miss of +0.138 arcsec. Keep this anchor even if a better-sourced value for the same epoch is found later; replace its value, not its role.

deferred.reason:
Both epochs ACQUISITION.md §4 asks for are recorded, so nothing is outstanding to make this file useful. What remains is an UPGRADE of provenance, not a gap in coverage: both values reach this file through secondary sources, and both would be stronger read off the primary publications. Neither is blocked on network egress — both blockers are that the primary sources are print.

One correction to ACQUISITION.md §4 belongs here rather than being silently absorbed: it suggests 1956-01-01 as the epoch, but the Calendar Reform Committee's defining instant is the 1956 VERNAL EQUINOX, 21 March, 0:00 ET. The ayanamsa moves ~50 arcsec/year, so those two dates differ by roughly 11 arcsec — several times this anchor's whole tolerance. Anyone re-deriving the value must take the epoch from the source and not from the suggestion.
provenance_upgrades: lahiri-mean-j2000 — confirm the constant 85885.53192 arcsec directly against the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris (Positional Astronomy Centre, Kolkata; print, ~annual). The present source is a peer-reviewed paper that ATTRIBUTES the constant to the IAE and is demonstrably careless in its own worked examples. Confirming it against the IAE would also settle, rather than merely argue against, the circularity question recorded in lahiri-true-1956-vernal-equinox's independence_note.

lahiri-true-1956-vernal-equinox — read the value off the Report of the Calendar Reform Committee (Government of India / CSIR, 1955) and its 1985 revision. Record which of the two figures is being cited, and keep the frame statement: the secondary source is explicit that the revised value is TRUE (nutation included), and that fact is load-bearing for how this anchor is compared.
deferred.still_unacquired_elsewhere: ACQUISITION.md §1 (planetary longitudes from JPL Horizons) and §3 (eclipses) remain unacquired. Horizons was NOT reachable when ACQUISITION.md was written but IS reachable now — it answered 200 during this session. That is the next anchor to take, and it is the one that would give the directory real coverage: ayanamsa and ΔT together constrain the frame and the clock, but nothing here yet checks a single planet's position against an external ephemeris.
